title: Ideas That Shaped Modern Politics
tagline: Liberalism, conservatism, nationalism, socialism and fascism, read beside the thinkers who framed them.
intro: Most of the political ideologies still argued over today took shape between the late 17th and the early 20th centuries. Liberalism grounded lawful government in the consent of the governed, and conservatism answered the French Revolution with tradition, authority and hierarchy. Nationalism held that each nation should govern itself, socialism and communism called for common ownership, and reformists sought equality through gradual democratic change. Fascism, born in Italy during World War I, exalted the nation above all and drove the Axis powers to war and genocide.

steps.why: Locke argued that government rests on the consent of the governed and must protect life, liberty and property, and his Two Treatises shaped liberal political thought.
Arising in 17th-century England and the Enlightenment, liberalism was used to justify the Glorious, American and French revolutions, and later split into classical and social forms.
A Whig who backed conciliation with the American colonies, Burke became a founding figure of modern conservatism with his Reflections on the Revolution in France of 1790.
Conservatism defends the established institutions of its time, in forms ranging from Disraeli's One Nation Toryism and Bismarck's welfare state to Salazar, Franco and Christian democracy.
Nationalism holds that a nation should govern itself; it drove Italian unification and the independence of Africa and Asia, and is often cited as a cause of both world wars.
Published in London in February 1848, the pamphlet of Marx and Engels cast all history as the history of class struggles and predicted a classless society.
From the October Revolution of 1917 communist governments spread until more than a third of the world lived under them, marked by one-party rule and the suppression of opposition.
Bernstein's Evolutionary Socialism (1899) disputed Marx's predicted collapse of capitalism and argued for gradual reform, which the SPD condemned but largely followed in practice.
Mussolini founded Fascism and ruled Italy as dictator from 1922 until 1943, invading Ethiopia in 1935 and allying himself with Nazi Germany.
Fascism sought a totalitarian one-party state; the wars and genocides of the Axis powers, the Holocaust above all, left it almost universally condemned after 1945.

title: Forms of Government through History
tagline: From chiefs and city-states to parliaments and single parties: how peoples have been governed.
intro: Peoples have been governed in many ways, and the same forms recur across continents and ages. A chiefdom joined villages under a hereditary chief who ruled through kinship, ritual and tribute; city-states from Sumer to Venice governed themselves and their countryside; Athens let its citizens decide in an assembly, and Rome elected its magistrates. Medieval lords and vassals divided power among landholders, early modern kings claimed it whole, and England's Bill of Rights bound the crown by law. The path ends with parliamentary democracy, born in 18th-century Britain, and the one-party state, which began in Soviet Russia after 1918.

steps.why: A chiefdom rules through kinship, ritual and tribute rather than officials, a standing army or written law, and arose independently from Mesopotamia to Polynesia.
Cahokia, built from about 1050 opposite present-day St Louis, raised Monks Mound, about 30 metres high and the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas.
A city-state governs itself and its countryside with its own gods, laws and army, a form found in Sumer, Greece, among the Maya and in medieval Italy.
Athens was governed directly: citizens attended the assembly by right and most officials and large juries were chosen by lot, though only free adult men took part.
From 509 to 27 BCE Rome was ruled by elected magistrates, Senate and assemblies, until civil wars from Sulla to Caesar and Octavian ended in monarchy under Augustus.
Feudalism bound vassals to lords by oaths of homage and fealty in return for fiefs, leaving power divided among landholders until France abolished it in 1789.
Louis XIV, King of France from 1643 to 1715, reigned at the height of royal absolutism, while his minister Colbert expanded France's colonies, navy and trading companies.
The Bill of Rights 1689 forbade the crown to suspend laws or levy taxes without Parliament's consent, and remains a cornerstone of the British constitution.
Between the 1720s and the 1830s real executive power in Britain passed from the monarch to a prime minister and cabinet answerable to the House of Commons.
The one-party state began in Soviet Russia between 1918 and 1921 and spread to Fascist Italy, Nazi Germany and many new states; most became multi-party after 1989–1991.

title: Abolition and the End of Slavery
tagline: Campaigners, writers and the enslaved themselves, and the laws that ended slavery in the Americas.
intro: Between 1787 and 1888 legal slavery was ended throughout the Americas. Abolitionism grew from Quaker and evangelical protest into campaigns of petitions, boycotts and public testimony, aimed first at the Atlantic slave trade and then at slavery itself. The enslaved fought for their own freedom throughout: in Saint-Domingue their revolution destroyed slavery and founded Haiti, and in the United States people who had escaped slavery led the campaign against it. The path runs from London's abolition society of 1787 to Brazil's Golden Law, after which freedom rarely brought the formerly enslaved land, compensation or equality.

steps.why: Abolitionism grew from Quaker and evangelical protest into the first great campaigns of petitions and boycotts, and between 1787 and 1888 ended legal slavery across the Americas.
Clarkson helped found the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade in 1787 and gathered evidence from sailors and ports for Wilberforce's campaign.
Equiano bought his freedom in 1766 and told Granville Sharp of the Zong massacre; his Interesting Narrative of 1789 helped win support for the Slave Trade Act of 1807.
France's richest colony took in some 790,000 to 860,000 enslaved Africans, who rose in 1791, saw slavery abolished in 1793 and beat the French army at Vertières in 1803.
A formerly enslaved man, Toussaint led the revolutionary forces and governed the colony until Napoleon's expedition captured him; he died in a French prison in 1803.
Wilberforce introduced abolition bills in Parliament from 1789 until the Slave Trade Act passed in 1807, then campaigned for the abolition of slavery itself.
The Act of 1833 abolished slavery in most of the British Empire after an apprenticeship period, and compensated the slave owners, not the enslaved.
Douglass escaped slavery in Maryland in 1838; his Narrative of 1845, his newspaper and his speeches drove the campaign against slavery in the United States.
After escaping in 1849 Tubman made some thirteen missions back to rescue about seventy people, and in the Civil War guided the Combahee Ferry raid that freed more than 700.
Coffee grown by enslaved people drove Brazil's wealth; Princess Isabel signed the Lei Áurea in 1888, and the planters' lost support let an army coup end the empire in 1889.

title: Votes for Women
tagline: From Wollstonecraft's Vindication to the Swiss vote: the long campaign for women's suffrage.
intro: The organised campaign for women's votes is usually dated from the Seneca Falls Convention of 1848, and it won its first national victory in New Zealand in 1893. Suffragists used petitions, conventions, lobbying and marches, and in Britain the militant suffragettes smashed windows, set fires and went on hunger strike. Much of Europe and North America gave women the vote around the First World War, while many women of colour and colonial subjects waited decades longer. This path begins with the feminist argument of the 1790s and follows the campaigners and the laws to Switzerland, where women won the federal vote only in 1971.

steps.why: In A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) Wollstonecraft argued that women only appeared inferior because they lacked education, and should be treated as rational beings.
Since the late 18th century feminist movements have campaigned for women's right to vote, hold office, work and own property; the suffrage movements were their first wave.
The first women's rights convention, held in July 1848, adopted a Declaration of Sentiments, and its resolution on suffrage passed after Frederick Douglass spoke for it.
Anthony founded the National Woman Suffrage Association with Elizabeth Cady Stanton in 1869, and used her trial for voting in 1872 to argue for women's citizenship.
Sheppard organised three petitions between 1891 and 1893, the last signed by 31,872 women, before New Zealand became the first self-governing country where women could vote.
From 1848 to 1971 suffragists used petitions, conventions, lobbying and marches, and won women the vote and the right to stand for election in most of the world's states.
Pankhurst founded the Women's Social and Political Union in 1903, whose suffragettes turned from processions to window-smashing and arson; she was imprisoned repeatedly.
Passed at the end of the First World War, the Act gave most women over 30 the vote for the first time and nearly tripled the United Kingdom's electorate.
Ratified in August 1920, the amendment barred denying citizens the vote on account of sex, though many women of colour remained excluded from voting in practice.
Swiss citizens decide by referendum and in open-air assemblies, and only in 1990 did the Federal Supreme Court order Appenzell Innerrhoden to admit women to its Landsgemeinde.
